config.title: Subarrays with K Distinct

intro.title: Subarrays with K Distinct
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that counts the number of subarrays with exactly K distinct integers in a given array. You will learn the sliding window technique, a core algorithmic pattern for efficiently processing contiguous sequences. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, objects (for counting), and loops. By the end, you'll understand how to apply this technique to solve a common interview lesson step by step.
intro.usecase: The subarrays with K distinct pattern is essential for analyzing sequential data in real-world applications like e-commerce analytics dashboards, where you might need to count all product view sequences containing exactly K different categories. It's used in content moderation systems to identify comment sections with exactly K unique users in sliding time windows, or in streaming services to find segments of a playlist where exactly K distinct genres appear. This algorithm helps developers implement sophisticated filtering and segmentation features in data-intensive applications where understanding specific diversity patterns within sequences is critical.

objectives: Implement a sliding window algorithm to track distinct elements in subarrays
Construct a frequency map to count occurrences of elements within the window
Manipulate window boundaries to maintain exactly K distinct elements
Apply conditional logic to expand and contract the window based on distinct count
Initialize and update counters for distinct elements as the window moves
Integrate the sliding window solution to count all valid subarrays
Control edge cases when K is zero or larger than the array length

content.body: Have you ever tried to count all the unique items in a shopping cart? In this lesson, we'll learn how to count subarrays with exactly K distinct elements. This is a common pattern in data analysis and string processing.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain what makes a subarray have exactly K distinct elements
2. Implement a solution using the sliding window technique
3. Use a hash map to track element frequencies
4. Count valid subarrays efficiently in one pass
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Look at this array:
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: How many subarrays have exactly 2 distinct elements?
content.successMessage: Great! You found that [1,2], [2,1], and [1,2,1] all have exactly 2 distinct elements.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now with 5 elements, how many subarrays have exactly 2 distinct elements?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You manually counted subarrays like [1,2], [2,1], [1,2,1], and many more.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: How many subarrays have exactly 3 distinct elements in this array?
content.successMessage: Well done! You checked many combinations to find all subarrays with exactly 3 unique elements.

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you looked at every possible subarray and counted distinct elements for each one. For small arrays, this works, but it becomes very slow for larger data.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 1000 elements, there are over 500,000 possible subarrays! Checking each one separately would be extremely slow. We need a smarter approach. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to remember which elements we've seen and how many times they appear. This lets us track distinct counts without rescanning the entire subarray each time.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. Each time we add or remove an element from our window, we update our notebook.

content.body: We'll use a sliding window with two pointers and a frequency map. The key insight: subarrays with exactly K distinct elements = (subarrays with at most K distinct) - (subarrays with at most K-1 distinct).
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For array [1,2,1,2,3], K=2:
1. Count subarrays with ≤2 distinct: expand window while distinct ≤2, count all subarrays
2. Count subarrays with ≤1 distinct: same process
3. Subtract: (≤2) - (≤1) = exactly 2 distinct
We use a frequency map to track counts efficiently.

content.body:
Here's our plan:
1. Create a helper function that counts subarrays with at most K distinct elements
2. Use two pointers (left and right) to define our window
3. Maintain a frequency map to track element counts in the window
4. Expand the right pointer, updating the map
5. When we have more than K distinct, shrink from the left
6. Count valid subarrays as we go
7. Use the formula: exactly K = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to count subarrays with exactly K distinct elements using the sliding window technique and frequency maps. Remember: the key insight is converting 'exactly K' to 'at most K minus at most K-1'. This pattern of using a lookup structure to remember what we've seen appears in many array and string lessons. Keep practicing with different values of K to build your intuition!
